title: Briefing: Albania, Serbia, France and India
script: Good morning. It's Saturday, November seventh, and this is the Unowned briefing: the stories that matter, checked and graded. It's read by a synthetic voice, and every fact comes from our published timelines.
Every item carries our grade. Confirmed means independent outlets agree. Reported means one source so far. Disputed means the accounts conflict. And alleged is one side's claim.
Here are the top stories.
Albania. Today: new developments in Albania's student protests.
Serbia. On Thursday: new developments in Serbia's student movement.
France. On Thursday: new developments in France's high school protests.
India. On Thursday: new developments in the Cockroach Janta Party movement.
Italy. No new developments since Wednesday, November fourth.
South Africa. No new developments since Wednesday, November fourth.
Canada. No new developments since Monday, November second.
Germany. No new developments since Monday, November second.
Now the details.

Albania. Today: Clashes broke out outside Prime Minister Edi Rama's office in Tirana on November seventh, with police using water cannons and tear gas, and protesters throwing fireworks and stones and, the Albanian Daily News says, Molotov cocktails, the paper reports. It gave no arrest or injury figures and no statement from police, the government or organisers. Our grade: reported. It rests on one source, Albanian Daily News, and isn't yet confirmed by a second.

Serbia. On Thursday, November fifth: Serbia's Republic Electoral Commission announced final results of the October twenty-fifth parliamentary election on November fifth: the Student List won 140 of 250 seats, President Vučić's list 103, and minority lists seven, with turnout about 68.8%, Xinhua reports. The outgoing speaker must convene the new parliament within 30 days, and a prime minister nominee needs a majority to form a government. We grade that reported: so far only Xinhua has it, and we're waiting for independent confirmation. Coming up: Formation of the new government and the choice of prime minister, the outcome of the Kričak detention.

France. On Thursday, November fifth: The FSU teachers' union said on Bluesky and Instagram that the strike was a majority one in lower and upper secondary schools and that nearly 1.6 million people marched; the CGT said on Telegram that 1.6 million were mobilised. Both unions urged further action. That's their own claim, posted on their channel, and we grade it alleged. Also on Thursday: About thirty masked people entered the Lycée Françoise in Tournefeuille, near Toulouse, at around 7:40 AM on November fifth and set fires and caused heavy damage, Le Monde reported. We grade that reported: so far only Le Monde has it, and we're waiting for independent confirmation.

India. On Thursday, November fifth: Union Minister Jitendra Singh alleged at a press conference in Bengaluru on November fifth that CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke received money from US-based donors and co-founder Ashutosh Ranka from Pakistani politicians, saying there was enough evidence. The CJP questioned the credibility of officials making the claim, and Congress leader Priyank Kharge asked the government to produce proof, Outlook India, India Today and News18 reported. Our grade: alleged. That's a claim by one side that no one has independently confirmed. Coming up: The Special Executive Magistrate hearing for the CJP leaders summoned over the Jantar Mantar protest listed for the third week of November.
Also on our watch, with no new developments in recent days.

Italy. The latest report, from Wednesday, November fourth: The national coordinator of the Rete degli Studenti Medi school-student network tells la Repubblica that the government should invest more in schools, and that fewer staff would lower the quality of teaching. We grade that reported: so far only la Repubblica has it, and we're waiting for independent confirmation.

South Africa. The latest report, from Wednesday, November fourth: The South African Government said on X, on local-election day, that asylum seekers and refugees may not vote. That's the authority's own claim, from its official statement, and we grade it alleged until independent reporting backs it up.

Canada. The latest report, from Monday, November second: Nine British Columbia First Nations announce Federal Court applications to quash the Pacific Link national-interest designation, saying Ottawa did not adequately consult them. We grade that confirmed: independent outlets report it.

Germany. The latest report, from Monday, November second: Germany's Education Minister Karin Prien calls the concerns of the young people who marched in more than 30 cities on October thirty-first "legitimate and extremely relevant" and promises more dialogue, and SPD politicians call for a national education summit. Our grade: reported. It rests on one source, The Local Germany, and isn't yet confirmed by a second.
We'll bring you updates on those as soon as they become available.

Coming up in the days ahead. Tuesday, November tenth, South Africa: The new asylum appointment system Home Affairs said would be in place by November tenth. Saturday, November fourteenth, Germany: Gen Z regelt plans another countrywide protest on November fourteenth, according to Bloomberg. Sunday, November fifteenth, Canada: Whether binding Pathways carbon-storage agreements are signed by the November fifteenth target. Monday, November sixteenth, Italy: The USB union said on Instagram that it will hold a 24-hour national strike of social-cooperative and social-enterprise workers in the health, care, education and job-placement sectors on Monday, November sixteenth, with a Rome rally at 10am, demanding pay rises, the return of welfare services to public bodies and better working conditions.
That's the Unowned briefing for Saturday, November seventh. Full timelines, and every source, are at unowned news dot com. Thanks for listening.
